questions.q: Under Section 3(1) of the Employee's Compensation Act 1923, an employer is NOT liable to pay compensation if the injury does not result in total or partial disablement for a period exceeding:
questions.src: Employee's Compensation Act 1923, Section 3(1); confirmed across multiple case-law summaries (legalserviceindia.com, ipleaders)

questions.q: The 'Doctrine of Notional Extension' under the Employee's Compensation Act 1923 primarily deals with:
o: Extending the employer's liability period after retirement
Extending the scope of 'in the course of employment' beyond the strict workplace/hours in appropriate circumstances
Extending compensation payments over a longer time period
Extending coverage to family members of the employee
questions.src: Doctrine of Notional Extension — settled principle, multiple sources including lawbhoomi.com, legalserviceindia.com

questions.q: In Moondra & Co. v. Mst. Bhawani, a truck driver died from burns after lighting a matchstick inside a fuel tank (with employer's permission) to locate a leak. The court held:
o: The employer was not liable as the driver acted negligently
The dependents were entitled to compensation as the accident occurred at the time and place of work
No compensation was payable as lighting a match was an 'added peril'
The insurance company alone was liable, not the employer
questions.src: Moondra & Co. v. Mst. Bhawani — cited consistently as the leading Notional Extension case (ipleaders, legalserviceindia)

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognised defence available to an employer under the Employee's Compensation Act 1923?
o: Willful disobedience by the employee of an order expressly given for securing safety
The employee earned less than minimum wage
The injury occurred on a public holiday
questions.src: Employee's Compensation Act 1923, Section 3(1) proviso; confirmed by legalserviceindia.com, ipleaders.in

questions.q: The 'Doctrine of Added Peril' as a defence for the employer applies when:
o: The employee is injured while performing normal assigned duties
The employee voluntarily undertakes an act outside the scope of his duties, adding danger not sanctioned by the employer
The employer fails to provide safety equipment
The employee is injured due to a natural disaster
questions.src: Doctrine of Added Peril — Devidayal Ralyaram v. Secretary of State cited as leading case (legalserviceindia.com)

questions.q: Under the Employee's Compensation Act 1923, can an employer plead 'contributory negligence' by the employee as a complete defence to avoid paying compensation?
o: Yes, contributory negligence is always a complete bar to compensation
No — the Act imposes liability irrespective of negligence; mere negligence or carelessness by the employee does not exempt the employer
Only if the negligence was intentional
Only in cases of death, not disablement
questions.src: Settled principle — Act excludes ordinary tort defences (contributory negligence, common employment, volenti non fit injuria) except for the specific statutory exceptions in Section 3(1) proviso

questions.q: As of the current wage ceiling in force (since January 2017), an employee is covered under the ESI Act 1948 if their gross monthly wages do not exceed ₹21,000 (₹25,000 for persons with disabilities). This ceiling amount is:
o: Revised annually by the ESI Corporation
Unchanged since 1 January 2017, confirmed still in force as of 2026
Abolished under the Code on Social Security 2020
questions.src: ESIC official coverage page (esic.gov.in): wage ceiling ₹21,000/month (₹25,000 disability), effective 01.01.2017, confirmed unchanged as of 2026 by multiple sources including Lexology legal analysis

questions.q: Under Section 1(2) read with Section 2(12) of the ESI Act 1948, the Act generally applies to non-seasonal factories employing:
questions.src: ESIC official coverage page: 10 or more persons (some states extend coverage differently for shops/establishments)

questions.q: As of the current contribution rates (in force since 1 July 2019), the total ESI contribution is 4% of wages, split as:
questions.src: ESIC/multiple payroll-compliance sources confirm: Employer 3.25%, Employee 0.75%, effective 1 July 2019

questions.q: Under the ESI Act, an insured woman employee is entitled to fully paid maternity leave for:
questions.src: ESI Act maternity benefit — 26 weeks, funded through ESIC, subject to minimum contribution period

questions.q: Administrative work assigned by the ESI Corporation, including day-to-day functions between Corporation meetings, is carried out by the:
questions.src: ESI Act structure — Standing Committee performs administrative/executive functions on behalf of the Corporation

questions.topic: ESI Act — Relationship with Employee's Compensation Act
questions.q: If an employee is covered under the ESI Act 1948, can they also separately claim compensation under the Employee's Compensation Act 1923 for the same employment injury?
o: Yes, they can claim under both Acts simultaneously
No — an employee covered under ESI cannot claim under the Employee's Compensation Act for the same contingency; the two are mutually exclusive for that injury
Only if the ESI claim is rejected first
Only for permanent disablement, not temporary
questions.src: Settled principle — ESI coverage excludes concurrent Employee's Compensation Act claims for the same risk, to avoid double benefit

questions.q: The standard formula for calculating gratuity under the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 for an employee not covered under a seasonal establishment is:
questions.src: Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 — standard formula: 15/26 × last drawn wages × years of service; confirmed across multiple sources including labourlawreporter.com

questions.q: Under the traditional eligibility rule of the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, a permanent employee (not on fixed-term contract) must generally complete how many years of continuous service to become eligible for gratuity?
questions.src: Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 — 5 years continuous service is the standard eligibility threshold for permanent employees

questions.q: The maximum tax-exempt ceiling on gratuity payable to an employee in the private sector under the Act is currently:
questions.src: Payment of Gratuity Act — ₹20 lakh ceiling, confirmed by labourlawreporter.com and multiple current sources

questions.q: Under the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, gratuity payable to an employee can be wholly or partially forfeited if the employee's services were terminated for:
o: Riotous or disorderly conduct, or an act of violence, or an offence involving moral turpitude committed in the course of employment
questions.src: Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, forfeiture provisions — riotous/disorderly conduct, violence, or moral turpitude offences in the course of employment

questions.q: Under the Payment of Gratuity Act 1972, an employer is required to pay gratuity to an eligible employee within how many days of it becoming payable?
questions.src: Payment of Gratuity Act 1972 — 30-day payment requirement, confirmed across sources; delay attracts interest

questions.q: Which of the following correctly ranks the three wage concepts from LOWEST to HIGHEST in terms of purchasing power/living standard, as traditionally understood in labour economics?
o: Fair Wage < Living Wage < Minimum Wage
Minimum Wage < Fair Wage < Living Wage
Living Wage < Minimum Wage < Fair Wage
Minimum Wage < Living Wage < Fair Wage
questions.src: Standard labour law concept — Minimum Wage (bare subsistence) < Fair Wage (better than minimum, some comforts) < Living Wage (best standard, full comforts); confirmed by OU LSF notes and standard labour law texts

questions.q: Under the Payment of Wages Act 1936, if the number of workers employed in an establishment exceeds 1,000, wages must be paid on or before which date of the following month?
questions.src: Payment of Wages Act 1936 — establishments with 1000+ workers: wages by the 10th; smaller establishments have an earlier deadline

questions.q: Under maternity benefit provisions, paid maternity leave of 26 weeks applies to a woman with how many surviving children?
o: Two or fewer surviving children (12 weeks otherwise)
questions.src: Maternity Benefit provisions — 26 weeks for women with two or fewer surviving children; 12 weeks for subsequent children beyond that

questions.q: Under maternity benefit law, dismissing or discharging a woman employee on the ground of her pregnancy, or during her period of maternity leave, is:
o: Permitted if she has less than 1 year of service
Prohibited — she is protected from dismissal on the ground of pregnancy/maternity leave
Permitted only in factories, not offices
questions.src: Maternity Benefit provisions — protection from dismissal on grounds of pregnancy is a core, stable protection

questions.q: Under Section 3 of the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, employment of a child (below 14 years) is:
o: Permitted in all family enterprises without restriction
Prohibited in any occupation or process, subject to a narrow exception for family enterprises/entertainment under specified conditions
Permitted for up to 4 hours a day in any occupation
Permitted with parental consent in any occupation
questions.src: Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act 1986, Section 3 — prohibition with narrow, conditional exceptions

questions.topic: Factories Act — Working Hours for Women
questions.q: Under Section 66(b) of the Factories Act 1948, as a general rule, no woman worker is permitted to work in a factory between:
questions.src: Factories Act 1948, Section 66(b) — general restriction on night work for women between 7 PM and 6 AM (subject to state exemptions in some cases)

questions.q: The Code on Social Security 2020 consolidates several existing labour welfare Acts (including the Employee's Compensation Act, ESI Act, Maternity Benefit Act, and Payment of Gratuity Act) into a single code. It was notified and brought into force with effect from:
questions.src: Multiple 2025-2026 sources confirm: Code on Social Security 2020 notified effective 21 November 2025 (distinct from the BNS/BNSS/BSA criminal law codes, which took effect 1 July 2024)

questions.q: Under the Code on Social Security 2020, the gratuity calculation formula for an eligible employee, as compared to the earlier Payment of Gratuity Act 1972:
o: Has been completely changed to a new formula
Remains the same (15/26 × last drawn wages × years of service)
No longer applies — gratuity is now a flat amount
questions.src: Multiple 2025-2026 sources (numericaconsulting.com, labourlawreporter.com, itactuary.com) confirm the gratuity formula is UNCHANGED under the Code — this is a stable fact even amid the broader transition
